newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy to set stricter inflation, deficit-GDP goals. [CORRECTED 21:10 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Italy to set stricter inflation, deficit-GDP goals. [CORRECTED 21:10 GMT]

text.p: The Italian government is expected to tighten its inflation and deficit targets for 1998 when it releases its key three-year economic plan this week, union officials who had seen the draft proposals said on Wednesday.

The plan, known as the DPEF, is due to be announced on Friday and will set the centre-left government's budgetary goals for 1998-2000 as it strives to beat its economy into shape for Europe's planned single currency.

The DPEF will also give the size of planned deficit cuts to be contained in next year's budget and outline the proposals for welfare savings, which economists say are vital if Italy wants to be fit for European economic and monetary union.
One union source, speaking to Reuters on condition of anonymity, said the DPEF had set the deficit-to-gross domestic product target at 2.8 percent.
That level is below the 3.0 percent set by both the Maastricht Treaty as a condition for membership of the single currency and the government's previous target.
The DPEF draft also showed the government had trimmed its inflation forecasts, but was cautious on growth.

Sergio D'Antoni, leader of Italy's second biggest trades union confederation, Cisl, said Prime Minister Romano Prodi, Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi and other senior members for the government had told union leaders on Tuesday night that the DPEF would set an inflation target of 1.8 percent next year.
That contrasts with the 2.0 percent goal for 1998 set by the Treasury when it announced quarterly state accounts in March and follows sharp falls in Italian inflation over the past months.

Official consumer price index figures are due to be published on June 4 (corrects from Thursday) and preliminary data from 11 cities point to an annual rate of 1.5 percent or 1.6 percent in April, its lowest level since May 1969 when inflation was at 1.4 percent.

But D'Antoni said the GDP growth target was 2.0 percent next year, unchanged from a target set in March when the government revised its DPEF figures and scaled back an earlier goal that the economy should grow by 2.8 percent in 1998.
The new DPEF, due to be approved at a cabinet meeting on Friday, sets goals of 2.5 percent growth in 1999 and 2.7 percent in 2000 with inflation at 1.5 percent for 1999 and 2000.

Italy is bidding to prove it will meet the Maastricht goals and sustain healthy economic performance despite criticism from the European Commission that Prodi has failed to enact structural reforms to tame the unruly deficit in a lasting way.

D'Antoni said the DPEF would outline the government's plans to slice 25 trillion lire ($15 billion) off the public sector deficit in its 1998 budget by slashing spending by 17 trillion lire and boosting revenues by eight trillion lire.
But he rejected the proposal. "The unions want it (the breakdown) to be half-and-half," D'Antoni said.
Prodi's latest measures to lop 15.5 trillion lire off the deficit in a 1997 mini-budget were set to clear their final parliamentary hurdle later on Wednesday and become law.
That package brings to nearly 100 trillion lire ($60 billion) the total deficit cuts pushed through by Prodi in three bitter budgets since he took office one year ago.
Prodi saved the most contentious topic -- an outline of welfare cuts and curbs on crippling early retirement pensions -- for another meeting with union leaders on Thursday.

Union leaders have warned they will not accept unlimited welfare cuts to meet the deficit goal. The hard-left Communist Refoundation party, whose support secures Prodi's parliamentary majority, has refused any reduction in social spending.
